To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the shape of the interface in the detachment process is influenced by the static contact angle and the distance to the critical detachment condition, and that the surface tension is influenced by the distance to the detachment condition.
the shape of interfaces at pinch-off is a strong function of the distance to the critical Bond number, the static contact angle, and the equilibrium shape.

(1) the shape of the pendant drop at the moment of pinchoff can be approximated by the shape of a pendant drop with a static contact angle of 90^ and a Bond number that is 10-30% larger than the critical one, (2) the nonequilibrium contribution to the surface tension can be approximated with a linear function of the neck radius, and, finally, (3) the temporal evolution of neck radius can be approximated as a power law function
In summary, our research is concerned with
the numerical simulation of the buoyancy induced detachment of a wall-bound pendant droplet.

the development of a diffuse interface model that allows for the simulation of the detachment of wall bound emulsion droplets in the presence of a static contact line, and, in addition, the investigation of the interface shape at detachment and the nonequilibrium behavior of the surface tension.
the influence of static and nonequilibrium contact angles on the shape of the pendant drop interface during detachment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the static contact angle is a crucial quantity in the detachment process of an isolated, buoyancy driven pendant emulsion droplets, and that the static contact line is the only place where the static equilibrium condition of the interface is not met.

, in the present context of buoyancy driven detachment, the static contact angle dependence on the critical Bond number is determined by nonequilibrium effects, while the static stability analysis of the equilibrium shapes is only valid at the critical condition.

the critical Bond numbers determined by our diffuse interface model are in good agreement with sharp interface models based on the Young Laplace theory, whereas the static contact angle dependence is in disagreement.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we can now explain the discrepancy between the critical Bond number as a function of contact angle for static stability and the critical Bond number for detachment as a function on contact angle, as well as the temporal evolution of neck radius in the detachment process, based on our phase field model.

the critical detachment condition is not only determined by the static contact angle and the critical Bond number but also by the nonequilibrium effects of the surface tension and the interface shape in the vicinity of detachment.
we are able to simulate the entire detachment process of a wall bound emulsion drop from the moment of pinchoff up to the moment of drop detachment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the static stability analysis of Young Laplace equation based equilibrium shapes does not capture the influence of static surface contact angle on the critical Bond number for detachment.
, in the case of a wall bound drop, the static contact angle dependence is not as strong as in the case of the free pendant drop, but still significant.
the critical Bond number of detachment is a function of the static contact angle, but not of the distance to the critical Bond number.
